newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Industry wants voluntary deal to stop chill cans.
newsitem.headline: Industry wants voluntary deal to stop chill cans.

text.p: Leading European chemical companies said on Friday they would seek support from the European Union for a voluntary agreement to rule out the use in self-cooling drinks cans of a refrigerant gas said to cause global warming.

The European Fluorocarbon Technical Committee (EFCTC) -- the trade body representing manufacturers of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) -- said it wanted a voluntary deal with refrigerants distributors and canned drink manufacturers not to use the HFC gas R134a in self-chill cans.
The hydrocarbon-based gas, planned for use in an innovatory drink can which has yet to hit the European market, is said to have a far more powerful effect on climate change than carbon dioxide (CO2).

Pressing a button at the base of the can releases the refrigerant gas into the atmosphere from a cannister inside it, chilling the contents by 30 degrees Fahrenheit (15 degrees Celsius) in about 90 seconds.

The European Commission said on Thursday it might consider banning the can, which was developed by the California-based Joseph Company, after EU environment ministers urged a probe into the possible effects of R134a on the ozone layer.
Senior EFCTC official Tim Vinks told Reuters the chemicals industry thought a voluntary agreement would be more effective than regulation because it would have the support of all sides.

Sales of R134a bring in billions of dollars to European chemicals firms like ICI, DuPont and Solvay for use in closed refrigeration and air conditioning systems, where it is not released into the environment.
"We wouldn't want this gas to have a bad name. There is a future for it in a contained situation," Vinks said, adding that the industry wanted to be seen to be acting responsibly.
He said it would be impossible to stop the use in self-chill cans of the gas, which is also produced by Japan, without the cooperation of distributors or can manufacturers.
He said few alternative chilling gases were suitable for this particular application and it would be better simply not to develop it.

The chief executive of Joseph Company, Mitchell Joseph, told Reuters on Thursday his invention would ultimately benefit, not harm, the environment by creating a whole new industry in self-cooling technology.
